name: Solar storm
explain: The Sun has thrown out a burst of charged particles. They can damage the electronics on board.
whatIsIt: A solar storm is a burst of charged particles from the Sun. It can flip bits in a computer or damage electronics.
realExample: In 2003 a huge solar storm forced NASA's Mars Odyssey orbiter to switch off its radiation instrument for good.
howCommon: Rare: a few big ones in each 11-year solar cycle
failText: The storm burned out the electronics. The spacecraft stopped answering.

options.label: Switch the instruments off until it passes
Keep working

name: Dust on the solar panels
explain: A dust storm has coated the solar panels. They make less power now.
whatIsIt: Mars has dust storms that can cover the whole planet. Dust on solar panels blocks the sunlight, so they make less power.
realExample: In 2018 a planet-wide dust storm covered the solar panels of NASA's Opportunity rover; it never woke up.
howCommon: Common on Mars in dust-storm season
protectedText: Your nuclear battery does not need sunlight. No power was lost.

options.label: Shake the panels clean (burns 5 kg of fuel)
Do nothing (power drops by 30%)

name: Course drift
explain: Tracking shows the spacecraft is slowly drifting off its planned path.
whatIsIt: No engine burn is perfect, and the Sun keeps tugging, so every spacecraft slowly drifts off its planned path. Tracking from Earth spots the drift early.
realExample: New Horizons fired its thrusters several times to fine-tune its path on the nine-year flight to Pluto, arriving in July 2015.
howCommon: Normal: almost every deep-space trip needs small corrections
failText: The spacecraft was off course and flew past {target}.

options.label: Correction burn (burns 8 kg of fuel)
Ignore it (3 in 10 chance of missing {target} on arrival)

name: Lost signal
explain: Earth has stopped hearing the spacecraft. The antenna may be pointing the wrong way.
whatIsIt: The spacecraft talks to Earth with a radio dish. If the dish points the wrong way, or the Sun sits in between, the signal is lost.
realExample: In October 2021 NASA stopped sending commands to all its Mars spacecraft for about two weeks, because the Sun sat between Earth and Mars and blocked the signal.
howCommon: Occasional: a few times per mission
protectedText: Your large dish antenna found Earth again.

options.label: Switch to the large dish antenna
Wait for Earth to call again
Point the antenna by guesswork (signal drops by 20% for the rest of the trip)

name: Instrument fault
explain: One of the science instruments has stopped working.
whatIsIt: Instruments are computers and sensors that must work for years in cold and radiation. Sometimes one just stops.
realExample: In 2021 the main payload computer of the Hubble Space Telescope failed; it switched to backup hardware and kept working.
howCommon: Occasional: most long missions lose one instrument

options.label: Reboot it (1 kg of fuel to turn the spacecraft, science drops by 10%)
Leave it off (science drops by 20%)

name: Debris warning
explain: Radar on Earth has spotted a piece of old space junk heading close to the spacecraft.
whatIsIt: Earth is surrounded by old rocket parts and broken satellites. Ground radar tracks the big ones and warns a spacecraft when one is coming close.
realExample: In November 2021 a satellite was blown up in a weapons test and the crew of the International Space Station had to shelter in their capsules while the cloud of pieces went past.
howCommon: Common near Earth — the space station moves out of the way a few times every year
protectedText: The big bus took the hit on its shielding.

options.label: Move out of the way (burns 12 kg of fuel)
Wait one day for better tracking (the warning is usually a false alarm)
Hold course

name: Micrometeoroid strike
explain: A grain of space dust has hit the spacecraft at enormous speed.
whatIsIt: Space is full of grains of dust moving faster than a bullet. One of them can chip a mirror or punch a hole in a panel.
realExample: In May 2022 a dust grain bigger than anyone expected hit the James Webb Space Telescope and left permanent damage on one of its mirror segments.
howCommon: Small hits are constant; a damaging one is rare
protectedText: A spare instrument covered the damage.

options.label: Turn the instruments away from the dust stream
Keep collecting data

name: Sunlight is pushing the spacecraft
explain: Sunlight falling on the panels is slowly turning the spacecraft off its path.
whatIsIt: Light itself has a tiny push. Over months, sunlight falling on big solar panels slowly turns a spacecraft and nudges it off course.
realExample: After two of its steering wheels broke, NASA's Kepler telescope was balanced against the push of sunlight on its solar panels, and in 2014 it started a whole second mission that way.
howCommon: Always happening — every mission has to allow for it
failText: The push of sunlight had turned the spacecraft just enough to miss {target}.

options.label: Tilt the panels to balance the push (power drops 10%)
Correct with the thrusters (burns 6 kg of fuel)
Let it drift

name: Planetary protection rule
explain: The planned path could hit {target}, and the rules say a spacecraft must not carry Earth germs there.
whatIsIt: Mission rules say a spacecraft must not carry Earth germs to a world where life might exist. If the path could hit the planet, it has to be changed.
realExample: In 2017 NASA deliberately flew Cassini into Saturn to burn it up, so it could never crash into Enceladus, a moon with an ocean under its ice.
howCommon: Every mission to Mars or an icy moon has to follow this rule
failText: Mission control took control of the spacecraft and pushed it away from {target}.

options.label: Raise the flyby path (burns 10 kg of fuel)
Point the instruments away and keep the path
Ignore the rule

name: Free push from a planet
explain: A planet is in the right place for a close flyby that would give the spacecraft a free push.
whatIsIt: Flying close past a planet steals a little of the planet's speed and gives it to the spacecraft. It is free fuel, but the aim has to be near perfect and the longer path costs time.
realExample: NASA's Juno swung past Earth in October 2013 to pick up speed, and reached Jupiter in July 2016.
howCommon: Used by almost every mission to the outer planets
failText: The flyby aim was off and the spacecraft never reached {target}.

options.label: Take the flyby
Stay on the direct path

name: An asteroid is passing close
explain: A small asteroid will pass near the flight path. Turning to look at it is science nobody planned for.
whatIsIt: Sometimes a small world happens to sit near the flight path. Turning to look at it is extra science the mission never planned for.
realExample: On its way to a comet, Europe's Rosetta spacecraft turned aside to photograph the asteroids Šteins in 2008 and Lutetia in 2010.
howCommon: A lucky extra — a few missions get the chance

options.label: Turn and photograph it (burns 4 kg of fuel)
Stay on plan

name: The spacecraft switched itself off
explain: The spacecraft found something wrong, shut everything down and is waiting for instructions.
whatIsIt: When a spacecraft notices something wrong, it shuts down everything except the radio and waits for instructions. Engineers call this safe mode.
realExample: In October 2016 NASA's Juno spacecraft put itself into safe mode just before a close pass of Jupiter, and the science from that pass was lost.
howCommon: Occasional — most long missions do it at least once
protectedText: Your backup systems found the fault and woke it safely.

options.label: Run the full check-out before waking it
Restart it immediately

name: No dish free on Earth
explain: Every big dish on Earth is listening to another mission, so there is no way to send the data home right now.
whatIsIt: Only a handful of giant dishes on Earth can hear a spacecraft in deep space, and every mission has to share them.
realExample: Only one dish on Earth can send commands to Voyager 2 — a 70-metre antenna near Canberra — and when it went offline for repairs for eleven months in 2020 the spacecraft could not be told anything.
howCommon: Constant — dish time is booked months ahead
protectedText: Your large dish antenna got the data home faster than expected.
failText: The memory filled up and the computer crashed. The spacecraft was lost.

options.label: Wait your turn for a dish
Send the data slowly on the small dish
Store everything on board and send it later

name: A bug in the flight software
explain: The computer keeps restarting itself. Engineers on Earth have found a mistake in its program.
whatIsIt: A spacecraft is run by a computer, and its program can have mistakes that only show up in space. Engineers can send a new program across millions of kilometres to fix it.
realExample: Days after landing on Mars in 1997, NASA's Pathfinder kept resetting itself, until engineers on Earth found the bug and sent up new software that fixed it.
howCommon: Common — almost every mission updates its software in flight

options.label: Upload the fix and test it carefully
Patch it live
Work around it

name: Jupiter's radiation
explain: The spacecraft is entering belts of charged particles strong enough to destroy its electronics.
whatIsIt: Jupiter is wrapped in belts of charged particles trapped by its magnetic field. They are strong enough to destroy ordinary electronics in weeks.
realExample: NASA's Juno carries its computer inside a titanium vault about a centimetre thick, built only to keep Jupiter's radiation out.
howCommon: Certain at Jupiter — the question is only how much
protectedText: The big bus shielded the computer.
failText: The radiation destroyed the computer. The spacecraft stopped answering.

options.label: Shorten the time in the belts (burns 15 kg of fuel)
Shield the computer by shutting instruments down
Fly straight through

name: Damage found
explain: A panel is making less power than it should. A piece of debris hit it after all.
whatIsIt: A strike is often noticed only much later, when a panel stops making the power the plan expected.
realExample: Small strikes are usually only found later, when engineers see that a panel is making less power than it should.
howCommon: Only after a close pass that was not avoided

options.label: Work with less power
Spin the spacecraft to face the Sun better (burns 5 kg of fuel)

name: Aim check after the flyby
explain: Tracking shows the flyby changed the path slightly more than planned.
whatIsIt: A planet never gives exactly the push the plan expected, so the new path has to be measured and tidied up.
realExample: After every gravity assist, mission control tracks the spacecraft for weeks to measure exactly what the planet did to its path.

options.label: Clean-up burn (burns 7 kg of fuel)
The aim looks close enough

name: The new instrument is working well
explain: The asteroid pictures came out better than anyone hoped, and there is more to send.
whatIsIt: Data taken by chance on the way to a target is still real science, if there is time to send it home.
realExample: Data taken on the way to a target has often turned into science papers of its own.
howCommon: Only when an extra target was photographed

options.label: Send it all home
Keep to the schedule
